messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 51-year-old Oceania man, has been married for over two decades and works as a welder. On a fateful evening last year, he was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that forever changed his daily experiences and his perception of the world around him. The accident occurred when John was returning home from work. The vivid memory still haunts him: the sudden screech of tires, the overwhelming smell of gasoline mixed with alcohol, and the sickening crunch as his car collided head-on with another vehicle that had crossed into his lane. In the aftermath, John found himself trapped inside a mangled heap of twisted metal, unable to move due to severe injuries. Since then, certain triggers have become unbearable for John. The sight of cars involved in minor accidents or even just the sound of screeching tires can instantly transport him back to that terrifying moment. The smell of alcohol often lingers on his senses, bringing with it a flood of memories and an overwhelming sense of dread. Car sounds, whether distant honks or revving engines, send waves of anxiety through his body. When these triggers occur, John experiences full sensory reliving of the event. He feels as though he is back inside the car, reenacting the positions and movements from that night. The pain in his body, where injuries had once been fresh and raw, seems to resurface with each intrusive memory. These memories are not just visual; they are vivid experiences that encompass every sense, leaving him feeling utterly overwhelmed and trapped. The weight of these memories has significantly impacted John's daily life as a welder. The workshop is filled with the sounds of machinery and often the faint smell of gasoline from welding materials, which can trigger his traumatic memories. He has become increasingly isolated at work, avoiding conversations about recent accidents or even casual mentions of cars. His colleagues have noticed that he often appears distracted and anxious during shifts. John’s marriage has also been affected by these symptoms. At home, the sound of an ambulance siren in the distance can set off a cascade of intense reactions. He becomes visibly agitated and sometimes leaves the room abruptly to regain control over his emotions. His wife has become increasingly concerned about his mental state and the strain it places on their relationship. The most challenging aspect for John is the unpredictability of these triggers, which makes him constantly vigilant and wary in his everyday surroundings. What frightens him most is the fear that he will never be able to escape this cycle of reliving the event and being overwhelmed by the associated pain and distress. He knows that something needs to change but struggles with how to navigate through this maze of traumatic memories without becoming paralyzed. John’s recent decision to seek help stems from a growing realization that his quality of life has been severely diminished, both at work and in his personal relationships. His wife encouraged him to talk about what he is going through, hoping for some relief from the constant turmoil. As he begins this journey toward healing, John hopes to regain control over his reactions and find ways to live without being constantly haunted by the memories of that fateful night.
